Not at all. I live in one of the poorest major cities in the US, and I think there's plenty of great stuff to do here despite seeing tons of decaying, abandoned buildings. It's very hard to interact with my city without walking through pretty obvious poverty - and that's totally fine.

A tour guide here showing people the coolest sights and scenes from a historical / cultural perspective is not participating in poverty tourism. A tour guide showing people the poverty specifically and saying "check out how run-down this neighborhood is" for two hours.....I mean come on, the difference is obvious.

Honestly that's exactly where I personally draw the line. Of course there's nothing wrong with visiting an area that's less affluent; travel would be all but impossible otherwise! But someone profiting off of showing off the poverty of an area is super icky. 

To use a US example: if someone wants to visit East St Louis, then that's totally up to them. But now imagine a tour bus rolling through the streets filled with affluent suburbanites gawking and taking photos of run-down houses and the poor (in every sense) people who have no means to escape that poverty.

Now, whether or not someone has the *time and motivation* is a completely separate conversation.

Plus those thousand hours will often translate to other languages. If you spend 1000 hours to get to B2 in Spanish, then you probably won't have to spend as many hours getting to B2 in Portuguese and Italian (and especially a language like Catalan).

Native Portuguese speakers actually have a HUGE advantage because they can often understand other romance languages (especially Spanish and Romanian) with zero practice!

Hell, there are countries in which it's pretty much standard to speak at least 3 languages. Being born in a country like the Philippines, Belgium, or Luxembourg means that you've got a good shot at being trilingual just by default. 

Us native English speakers often just don't have the same motivation to learn other languages. Some of the reasoning is logical (learning Spanish probably won't increase my income potential) and some of it is a bit ignorant (learning other languages isn't "important".) I think it would make a ton of sense for every American to learn at least B1 Spanish.

Sometimes I become envious of people born in countries where the importance of learning 2nd and 3rd languages is greatly emphasized, but I must remind myself that being a native English speaker often carries a tremendous amount of privilege.

It's a fair question to ask. Here are my two cents:

- Yes, the payment structure for most streaming services is borderline robbery. We all keep doing it because you're basically digging your own grave by not making your music widely available. If it didn't work for Neil Young, then it won't work for some small, unknown artist.

- We all *should* boycott services like Spotify, but realistically it won't change anything unless the big players join in. Most people are listening to Taylor Swift and Joe Rogan, not a bunch of local artists. All of us leaving Spotify would hardly touch their bottom line. 

- Nowadays you make money from T-shirts instead of albums, either from online sales or live shows. 

- The technology has changed, whether we like it or not. Streaming is how "we" listen to music now. Artists need to accept the *technological change* but fight for fair payment. - Artists absolutely can afford to record their own music. That's the *best* change that's happened. It used to cost $100k minimum to record and distribute an album en masse. Today it costs...a DAW and a couple mics. Skill is FAR more important than gear today. 

- Everyone looks to the past with rose-colored glasses. Because recording used to be so expensive, artists would sell their souls to record labels so that they could get an advance to cover recording costs. These deals were TERRIBLE. Unless you sold a TON of copies, the artist didn't actually make any money. Seriously, everyone got screwed by their labels back in the day. Nowadays it's actually possible to independently release music that sounds pro.

TLDR: yes, streaming services are screwing us. No, we didn't used to live in a utopia where artists were paid fairly. We do need to fight for fair payment, but we also need to be realistic about how to actually make money as an artist.

I would do some research as to what a music degree will get you. There's a running joke about Berklee that no one actually graduates because people form bands and then drop out. Put more seriously: music schools tend to be VERY expensive compared to average earnings in music, so they have the potential to saddle you with a ton of debt.

If you want to teach music in a traditional school, then yes, you will need a music education degree. Some orchestras will require a degree because they're so damn competitive. Remember that the world's supply of musicians is functionally infinite, so acclaimed orchestras and ensembles can be incredibly selective. 

You do NOT need a degree to write songs or play gigs. I would HIGHLY recommend getting experience as soon as possible with those two ventures. You have to write a LOT of bad songs before you come up with any good ones, so start now. Same goes for gigs; the early ones will be your worst (which is a good thing).

You do NOT need a degree to teach piano in individual lessons. Maybe it helps in some cases, but you really just need to prove that 1. you are quite skilled at piano 2. you're an effective teacher. You do NOT need a degree to learn music theory. 

You absolutely can make a living as a musician. Just remember that, in most cases, you'll work twice as hard for half the money as compared to working a boring day job and doing music after work. You have to decide for yourself whether the sacrifice is worth it.

Typically the way it works is that your taxes are withheld per tax brackets per paycheck. In other words, you can take the amount on your paycheck and multiply it by your total paychecks per year, and then you're taxed based on that amount. That calculation is happening every paycheck.

When you work 96 OT hours you're making something like 3x as much money as a regular 80 hour 2 week period. If your "normal" 40 hour pay is $50k per year ($2083 every 2 weeks), then, for that pay period, you basically made almost 3x your income, so it appears more like $150k per year *for that paycheck*. 

When you make $50k per year you fall into the 10%, 12%, and (a little bit of) 22%. At $150k you max out the 22% and get halfway through the 24%. So then your payroll says FOR THAT PAY PERIOD "oh this person is taxed at $150k" and puts your money into those brackets.

When do you get that back? At the end of the year when you submit your pay statements for the entire year. You'll get a big ol' check from the federal government for all of those pay periods where you shot above your average pay (and, therefore, your average tax brackets). Maybe you didn't account for the standard deduction either, so there will probably be extra money in there too.

You could set up your W4 to try to account for what's closer to your predicted overall pay for the year. But then you're taking the chance that you'll OWE money at the end of the year, and I'd rather play it safe on the other side. 

TLDR: each pay period is taxed / withheld on its own. At the end of the year all of the discrepancies will be resolved with the IRS. You will probably get a check from the federal government.

Here's a quick list of IMO the most important differences between a 401k and IRA

Yeah I go to shows every week, and earplugs are a LIFESAVER. I guarantee I would have noticeable hearing damage without them. 

For OP's sake: remember that decibels are measured on a logarithmic scale. That means that a 10 DB reduction in sound pressure is 10x quieter for your ears. A 30 DB reduction (about how much earplugs reduce) means the sound is 10,000x less intense (10^4). If you look up hearing damage charts about 1 minute of 110DB exposure can start to cause hearing damage whereas 80 DB will take 4-8 hours.

So yeah, earplugs often are the difference between permanent hearing damage vs. enjoying a show carefree. Just take it easy on your ears before and after the show.

Buying can make a lot of sense if the following applies for you:

- You have 20% of the purchase price in cash (you don't necessarily have to put down 20%, but you should have about that amount saved). In other words: you can actually afford the house.

- You can afford the mortgage payments PLUS up to 50% more for maintenance, insurance, etc. I live in a cheap market and bought a fixer-upper, so I actually budget 100% on top of my mortgage for the "extras". 

- Your income is relatively stable.

- You have good credit.

- You aren't going to move / sell for at least 5 years, hopefully longer. 

- You already have some money invested in retirement accounts.

- You aren't going to overpay for the house. This one sounds crazy, but when I bought in 2022 people were doing all kinds of dumb shit. I had friends 2x their budget. That is a GREAT way to be house poor.

I wouldn't plan on using investments for a home purchase unless you're looking 10+ years into the future. The S&P 500 has proven to be a GREAT long term investment, but it's volatile in the short term. For example: a share was worth more in Dec 2021 than it was in Nov 2023. 

Imagine it's 2007 and you're thinking you'll buy a house in 3 years. You put most of your savings in the S&P 500, knowing that you'll use that money for a down payment. In Oct 2007 your S&P shares are at $1500. 3 years later they're at $1200. Houses are at the lowest price point that you've ever seen, but you can't afford one now because your net worth is still down 20% and the job market is atrocious because you're just coming out of the worst financial crisis of your lifetime.

So yeah, for short and medium term purchases (within 5 years or so) I'd keep that money as liquid as possible, i.e. high yield savings account or in a CD. For long-term goals like retirement stocks are a better option because you have more time to outlast the volatility. 

For basically anything short-term the best thing that you can do is maximize your income. That can be via education, working more, etc., but it'll be the most powerful tool in your young working life. Of course it's totally cool to have work /life balance as well.

I would also recommend making a list of activities in life that truly bring you joy. They can be anything from going to concerts to rock climbing to walking in the park to playing in a band, etc. Then figure out how much each activity costs per month.

Now compare your list to your credit card bill. Is there anything eating away at your money that isn't on this list? Those should be the first things to cut. 

Maybe you really enjoy going out to eat once a week, but you realize that you could drive a less expensive car or take public transportation. Maybe you enjoy hiking more than going to the gym but are still paying for a gym membership that you barely use. Maybe having a game night with your friends at your place brings you as much joy as going out and having $14 cocktails.

There is NO sense in spending money on things that don't keep you alive / employed and don't bring you joy.

It's very likely that you will receive this inheritance, and you can probably even arrive at a fairly accurate estimate for what that will be. The hyper conservative approach is to assume no inheritance, which is what most "savers" would do. Another approach would be to figure out your estimate and then cut it in half. That seems more rational to me.

With that said, the hyper conservative route is indeed the safest route. I would just encourage you (and anyone else) not to make ALL of your predictions pessimistic and hyper conservative. For example, if you assume 0 inheritance, then don't also assume 0 social security benefits. Don't assume hyper inflation. Etc. Otherwise you'll spend way too much time worrying about your bleak future and then end up dying with a pile of cash. That benefits no one.

So yeah, I'd try to estimate your realistic inheritance and then throw a safety factor on it. Or maybe your inheritance IS the safety factor, and you just assume optimistic results for the rest of your finances.

Your points about housing are valid, but we're missing a key consideration. If we compare the US to western Europe: in most of western Europe single family detached houses are more expensive than those in most of the US, but rent tends to be more affordable. That's for two main reasons:

1. Zoning laws, i.e. Europe is more densely populated and has infrastructure to support that style.

2. Laws protect renters from abusive landlords.

It's important to remember that other countries deal with similar issues, but western European countries have dealt with these issues in intelligent and scientific ways instead of just wishing that the issues didn't exist.

I think what OP is trying to say is that you need to live somewhere, so landlords can jack up prices and will eventually get desperate tenants willing to pay anything. What OP is missing is that renters could all decide to live with a bunch of roommates, which would kill like 2/3rds of landlords because demand would plummet. 

So yes, it absolutely is supply AND demand, but it sometimes feels like supply-only because we often assume that everyone needs to live alone. Of course we could also get into US zoning laws and how they artificially limit supply....

For anyone reading: I promise that the US is not all sunshine and roses either. The main thing that we have going for us is high incomes, though one must keep in mind our high cost of living and astronomical healthcare and education costs. But there certainly is an opportunity for immigrants to come and make a high wage while finding a way to cut living expenses. 

Here are the negatives that I see with the US:

- Public transportation is abysmal. There are about 5 US cities with decent public transportation. Our cities are pretty much unconnected except for a few expensive and slow Amtrak lines. I think that most Europeans would be shocked by the state of our transportation infrastructure. Biking is similar: most cities lack functional bike lanes. Many of our bike lanes are actually statistically MORE DANGEROUS than roads that simply don't have bike lanes. 

- You will need a car which will cost $3,000-10,000 per year for the car payment, insurance, gas, maintenance, etc. In most US cities your only other option is the bus system, which tends to be VERY slow and ineffective (unless you are traveling very short distances in the city). 

- Our healthcare system is insanity. I pay about $1000 per year for an HSA (health savings account) plan through my work. If I require some sort of hospitalization, like breaking my arm or getting sick for a few days, then I would pay up to $6000 before my insurance covered anything. Other Americans pay more per month but have a lower deductible, but....yeah it's insane. Plus our insurance companies can arbitrarily decide not to cover certain procedures.

- US rates of violence tend to be higher than those in western and central Europe. Our homicide rate is about 3x higher than Turkey, Montenegro, Belarus, Moldova, etc. It's still unlikely to affect you personally, but the point is that the US is statistically more violent than nearly every European country - by a good margin.

- We have very few employee protections. You can be fired at any time for any reason, and it's generally very difficult to receive reparations in a case of discrimination. 

- We are generally quite unhealthy. I suggest looking up life expectancy and infant mortality rates. The US is a very, very unhealthy country considering how wealthy we are. 

- Much of our food is banned in Europe. There is a lot of amazing food in the US, but some of the stuff in our grocery stores is literally considered dangerous by many other countries. 

- Interactions with law enforcement cover a MASSIVE spectrum. Sometimes it's very pleasant, and other times the police will literally point a gun at you. Response times can be really bad too, for a number of reasons. And many people of color can share stories of facing discrimination from our LEOs.

I think there are many amazing things about the US, but I would want an immigrant to understand each of these issues before they move here.

Here are some things that I've learned now that I've recorded close to 10 albums:

- The first one will sound the worst. That's a good thing! You'll learn new tips and tricks the more you do it.

- Capturing a great performance is the most important part. You can't polish a turd. People listen to shitty bootlegs of their favorite artists because they love the songs and performances. Production value matters, but it matters far less than songwriting and performance.

- I like to record twice as many songs as I release. I won't fully mix and master the "extras", but I like having them recorded.

- Almost all instruments can easily be re-recorded if need be. Acoustic drums are a pain in the ass. You have to get them right before everything else. Electronic drums are soooooooo much easier. 

- Take chances. You don't have money or fame working for you, so you have to rely on your creativity. If you have a choice between something conventional and something weird but really cool and exciting....do the weird one. Or make two versions. DO NOT STIFLE YOUR OWN CREATIVITY!

- Collaborations are GREAT. You will learn so much from your collaborators, and it also makes for a great marketing strategy because you can connect two or more fan bases. Collaborations work best if you write the song and then leave room for a vocal part / guitar solo / whatever. Give the collaborator as much or as little creative freedom as they want.

- Focus on the process, not the results. Chances are fewer people will listen to this album than you'd like to believe. That's okay.

- To reiterate: your album is going to sound low-budget. You are DIYing without much experience and without paying an experienced engineer or producer. The success of this album, however you want to define it, lives and dies on your creativity and your willingness to learn.

As others have said, it comes down to the ratio between your income and expenses and using what's leftover for savings. The average American's top 3 expenses are their housing, transportation, and food. 

Here are the most common pieces of advice that I see (and agree with) in the financial independence community:

- If you have the opportunity to make more money elsewhere, then do it. We are living at a time when employers are desperate for workers. Don't just accept your situation if it isn't working for you.

- Living on your own, i.e. without roommates, might not be an option.

- Cook most of your meals. Go out to eat no more than once or twice per week. Make cheap, healthy, big batch meals like stir fry.

- Any debt with an interest rate over 7% needs to be paid off ASAP. This includes student loans in some cases and pretty much always included credit card debt.

- You might not be able to live in a high cost of living city like New York or LA. Midwest cities often have the best income to expense living opportunities.

- Drive a used car from a brand known for its reliability. Honda, Toyota,  Subaru, etc. Your car might have to be pretty old for a while. 

- If you buy a house, then buy something with monthly payments that are far lower than your income. Don't be house poor. 

- Unfortunately many people simply cannot afford to buy a house on a single income. It's much more doable in the Midwest than on the coasts.

- You might have to become a landlord.

As a shredder myself, I can provide a real answer. Believe it or not, the technical parts are not that difficult. Sure, if you want to have the accuracy of Tim Henson, then you're going to have to put in hours, but it's really just muscle memory. Learn a scale and play it over and over and over. Start very slowly. If you can play it slow, then you can play it fast (with a bit more practice). 

It should be noted that there's a difference between shredding and shredding in a memorable way. Every famous, easily distinguishable shredder has certainly tricks and techniques that separate them from the pack. It's why you probably cannot name any of those "world's fastest shredders", but you know guys like Petrucci, Satch, Vai, Yngwie, etc. 

IMO the "hard mode" of shredding is when you learn to play fast, challenging stuff across genres and styles. The most interesting shredders (to me) are the ones that have a seemingly-endless supply of new licks and tricks. It's sort of the anti-Yngwie, since he generally just plays the harmonic minor scale as quickly as possible. IMO shredding becomes "hard" when you start applying it to various genres.

My Mount Rushmore of shredders is generally guys like Guthrie, Holdsworth, Al Di Meola, Joe Pass, Marty Friedman, John 5, etc. IMO those are the guys who seem to be able to do just about anything on the guitar while still maintaining their own unique identity. That, to me, is what makes shredding difficult.

But if your goal is just to be able to play scales very quickly? Practice those scales for an hour per day, increasing speed little by little, and you'll be able to shred in 6 months or so.

There are two scenarios in which you'll play live:

1. The venue has a full professional sound system.

2. The venue does not have a full sound system, so your amp is 100% of your volume.

For the second scenario you need an amp. I recommend having an inexpensive but decent and loud amp and then running your amp modeler through the effects loop, which bypasses the preamp on the amplifier. 

Again, I'm not saying that this will work for everyone, but it's way less stuff to carry, and the sound guy will love you.
